textContent: Native Indian Breeds A lot of good work has been done by many Indians, some of whom have spent their entire lifetime on the documentation of the Indian breeds. But unfortunately for us all the standard for many Indian breeds has not found common consensus. Only the more popular or rather the breeds that have more number of dogs have been studied, measured, and standards written for them. It is not the aim of this website to go into the details of the differing opinions or research the details of these standards. Though the site is called dogsindia.com because it is meant to be a database of info on all dogs and dog owners, breeders, vets and all members who provide dog related services in India, it is not just a site on Indian dogs alone. So we shall provide a summary of the info available with us on the individual native Indian dog breeds. If we are wrong please do write to us with your valuable suggestions. If you have detailed info or can help us find that info about some lesser known breeds such as the Kanni, the Manjil, and so on, please do help us by writing to us by e-mail or by regular mail. We shall be very thankful for your help. This is a tall breed with a noble carriage and short coat. The dogs may be red, fawn and black with white markings on their chest. The muzzle is black. The brisket is deep, and the limbs are well muscled. The back is long with the tail tapering to a fine point. The ears are set high on the skull and pricked. It has a long and graceful stride. The Kuchi is also a native of Thanjavur, but it is a small dog with a long coat. It is about 25cms in ht. and weighs about 7kgs. It is very thinly built. The tail is heavily feathered and curled up to look like a ball of hair over the short back.It is a good hunter of vermin. The Kaikadi is named after a nomadic tribe in Maharashtra. It may be white, tan, and black. The dogs are small (about 40 cms or less) with thin long legs, but powerful thighs and hocks. They make excellent watch dogs. They can hunt hare and vermin. The tail is long and tapering. The head is long and thin with prominent eyes and long ears that stand erect when alert. In India, more than 60 million stray dogs are living in animal shelters without a permanent home or family. Preconceptions against Indie dogs often deprive them of a loving home. The humble Indie dogs are subject to ingrained prejudices, with people preferring foreign breeds over their native counterparts. The Indie breed, also called the Indian Pariah dog, is among the world’s oldest dog breeds. They are highly intelligent, loyal, adaptable, and resilient. Native to the Indian subcontinent, they are perfectly suited to be part of an Indian family. Those who have gone ahead and adopted Indies can vouch for their amicable and lovable nature. Indie Dog Temperament & Adaptable Nature Known for their intelligence, loyalty, and adaptability Affectionate companions and good watchdogs Naturally healthy and low-maintenance compared to other pedigree dogs Social, energetic, independent, and territorial They are native breeds and highly adapted to the Indian climate. Most of the Indie dogs have a short, smooth coat, making grooming quite effortless. After an Indie dog adoption, all your pet needs is a nutritious diet, regular vaccinations, loving care, and daily exercise. Indie Native Dogs – Great Companions Pariah dogs have a loving and delightful nature. With more awareness about the breed, many pet lovers are coming forward to adopt them. These native dogs can quickly adjust to your surroundings and new lifestyle. They can prove to be great companions, especially for elderly people, young kids, and lonely individuals. Verified animal shelters such as Kannan Animal Welfare are wondrous facilities in Delhi that offer a wide range of Indie dogs and other Indian street dogs. Organizations like the Animal Welfare Board of India work towards improving the welfare and protection of animals across the country. Adopting from a rescue shelter can help reduce the number of homeless and lonely dogs. Native Dog Training Indies are real fast learners. These pets also respond better to some basic training and positive reinforcements. They can be introduced to simple puzzle games and obedience intrusion training. Training can keep them sharp and alert. Wherever you live, a township or a bustling city, in a small apartment or a big house, Pariah dogs adapt with ease. That is one of the reasons why they are becoming a favourite choice among potential pet parents. Intuitive & Empathetic With smart intelligence and an emotional nature, Indie dogs can sense human moods and behave accordingly. Many Indie parents love their emphatic and intuitive side and feel that these pure souls often go out of their way to comfort or relax their human family. Once they bond properly, their loyalty remains unshaken, and they become very protective of their families. They need socialisation, physical exercise, and good mental stimulation to maintain robust health. Indie Dog Care & Feeding Needs Indian native dogs are strong and low-maintenance pets. But, like all pets, they do need nurturing care and love to thrive. They also require physical workouts and regular health check-ups by a trusted vet, who can provide vaccinations and deworming. Grooming needs are minimal, as they have a trimmed coat. You can give them monthly baths to keep their skin clean, tick-free, and in good shape. Good nutrition plays a vital role in keeping them fit and healthy. Native dogs can flourish on simple home meals, which are nutritious, balanced, and dog-healthy. They have highly evolved digestive systems. Indie dog care includes a wholesome diet and avoiding unhealthy processed foods. You are not just saving a life, you are giving the voiceless soul another chance at being a part of a loving family. You can connect with Kannan Animal Welfare, a dedicated NGO and fill out their online application forms for adoption. A smooth and responsible rehoming process is initiated by KAW after gathering information about pet parents and their background. You can call or visit us for more details on Indie dog adoption. FAQs What is the average lifespan of an Indie dog? The average lifespan of Indian Pariah dogs can range between 12 to 16 years. While Indies are resilient and rarely get diseases, taking preventive measures like giving vaccinations, deworming, and using flea-tick control products always helps. Where can you find a large number of Indie dogs for adoption? You can search on social media platforms, local animal and rescue shelters, and verified NGOs to find and adopt Indie dogs. Do you feel Indie dogs are social creatures? Indies are naturally social, communicative, and smart. Once you train and socialise them, they can get along with all kinds of pets and other dogs. It is ensured that you will never find a dull moment in their company. How to fight against breed prejudice? Breed prejudice happens in India and many dogs fall victim to this practice. India is home to millions of homeless animals like cats and dogs. Most rescued dogs in shelter houses are natives or street dogs. Your decision to adopt such dogs can stop this inhuman breed prejudice against them. You will also get a loyal and loving furry friend for life. It will be like a god’s gift for them to get out of unsafe streets and overcrowded shelters. Why adopt Indian Pariah dogs? The native Pariah dogs are born survivors, they are also very intelligent, courageous, and full of love and joy. They do not cost much, need little grooming, are very healthy, and easily adapt to all types of small or big homes. All they want is some love and care. Adopting one can definitely reduce the homeless stray dog population and give them a real chance of belonging to a loving family.

The sandy-brown dog asleep under the chai stall outside your gate may belong to a canine lineage that has lived alongside people on the Indian subcontinent for generations. Yet when people search for Indian dog breeds, they often find the same handful of names, photos and descriptions about loyalty, intelligence and weather resistance. India’s native dogs are much more diverse than that. There are lean sighthounds built for speed, powerful property guardians, thick-coated Himalayan livestock dogs, village landraces and companion dogs. Some have formal recognition from government institutions or kennel clubs. Many others remain regional breeds or populations with little formal documentation. As of August 2026, six indigenous dog breeds have been registered through ICAR-NBAGR: Rajapalayam, Chippiparai, Mudhol Hound, Gaddi, Changkhi and Kombai. But official registration tells only part of the story. This guide looks at India’s best-known native dog breeds, what they were traditionally bred to do, how recognition works, and most importantly, what kind of home each dog actually needs. How Many Indian Dog Breeds Are There? There is no single universally agreed number of Indian dog breeds. Depending on how regional landraces, local populations and formally standardised breeds are counted, India has roughly 20 or more named native dog breeds and types. That difference matters because the term “Indian dog breed” can refer to several different things. A dog may be officially registered by ICAR-NBAGR, recognised within the pedigree or dog-show system, documented as a regional population, or exist as a naturally developed landrace such as the Indian Pariah Dog. So a breed does not suddenly become Indian only when an organisation issues it paperwork. Formal recognition is better understood as documentation of a population that already exists. Which Indian Dog Breeds Are Officially Registered? ICAR’s National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources, or NBAGR, documents and registers indigenous animal genetic resources in India. Dogs entered this national breed-registration system relatively recently. Rajapalayam, Chippiparai and Mudhol Hound became the first three native dog breeds registered by the bureau in 2020. Gaddi and Changkhi followed in 2025. In August 2026, Kombai became the sixth registered indigenous dog breed. Indian Dog Breed Home Region ICAR Registration Traditional Role Rajapalayam Tamil Nadu 2020 Hunting and guarding Chippiparai Tamil Nadu 2020 Sighthound and hunting Mudhol Hound Karnataka 2020 Hunting, guarding and sighthound work Gaddi Himachal Pradesh 2025 Livestock guarding Changkhi Ladakh 2025 High-altitude livestock protection Kombai Tamil Nadu 2026 Guarding and hunting Registration gives these breeds formal documentation and accession numbers and can support their study and conservation. It does not mean these are the only native dogs India has. ICAR Recognition and Kennel Club Recognition Are Not the Same Thing This distinction causes confusion in many articles about Indian dog breeds. ICAR-NBAGR registration focuses on documenting India’s indigenous animal genetic resources. Kennel club recognition works differently. It is generally concerned with breed standards, pedigrees, registration and dog shows. That means a breed can be recognised within one system without having exactly the same status in another. The Kennel Club of India has recognised several native breeds, including well-known names such as Rajapalayam, Chippiparai, Kanni, Kombai and Mudhol Hound. Then there are native dogs that fall outside these formal systems altogether. The Indian Pariah Dog is the most obvious example. Age, socialisation, training, health and the individual dog’s temperament can matter as much as breed. 1. Indian Pariah Dog or Indie The Indian Pariah Dog, commonly called an Indie or Desi dog, is one of India’s most familiar native dogs. It is generally considered a landrace rather than a modern pedigree breed created through a closed studbook. Typical Pariah-type dogs are medium-sized with erect ears, a wedge-shaped head, a short coat and an athletic build. But naturally occurring populations are not as physically uniform as tightly standardised pedigree breeds. One important distinction is worth making: An Indian Pariah Dog and a street dog are not necessarily the same thing. “Street dog” describes where a dog lives. It does not establish its ancestry. India’s free-ranging dog population contains Pariah-type dogs as well as dogs of mixed ancestry. What are Indies like as pets? Many Indies are intelligent, observant and highly adaptable. But there is no single “Indie temperament.” A puppy raised around people from an early age can behave very differently from an adult dog that has survived years of threats, traffic or conflict with other dogs. An adopted adult dog also has one practical advantage: its approximate size, personality and energy level may already be easier to judge. For many households looking primarily for a companion, an Indie can make more practical sense than acquiring a rare working breed because it looks impressive. You can learn more in our guide to the Indian Pariah Dog, or read why and how to adopt an Indian Pariah Dog. 2. Rajapalayam The Rajapalayam comes from Tamil Nadu and takes its name from the town of Rajapalayam. It is one of India’s most visually distinctive native breeds, particularly because of its tall frame and traditionally associated white coat. Historically, Rajapalayams were used for hunting and guarding. Those working origins matter when considering one as a pet. A dog developed to notice threats, pursue animals and work independently should not automatically be expected to behave like a breed developed primarily for companionship. Rajapalayams can form strong bonds with familiar people and may be reserved around strangers. Early socialisation, consistent training and responsible handling are therefore important. For many first-time dog parents living in small urban homes, a Rajapalayam may be more challenging than an Indie or a smaller companion breed. 3. Chippiparai The Chippiparai is a native sighthound from Tamil Nadu. Its narrow body, long legs, deep chest and lean frame reflect its traditional purpose: pursuing game across open terrain using speed and sight. That history can also translate into a strong instinct to chase. A Chippiparai therefore needs more than an occasional walk around the block. Owners need to think about physical exercise, mental stimulation, recall training and safe spaces where the dog cannot simply pursue a moving animal into traffic. They can be closely bonded with familiar people while remaining more reserved with strangers. For an active household that understands sighthounds, the Chippiparai can be fascinating. For someone looking for a low-energy apartment dog purely because native breeds are assumed to be “easy,” it may be a poor match. 4. Mudhol Hound The Mudhol Hound is one of India’s best-known native sighthounds and is particularly associated with Karnataka and the Deccan region. It is also known by the Caravan Hound name in historical and breed discussions. Mudhol Hounds were developed for speed, endurance, hunting and guarding work. Their ability is not purely historical. Indian security forces have also experimented with and deployed native breeds, including the Mudhol Hound, for working roles. That is an impressive demonstration of the breed’s athletic potential. It is also a reason not to treat the Mudhol as a decorative pet. An athletic working dog needs appropriate outlets for its energy. Mudhol Hounds generally make more sense for active owners who can provide consistent exercise, training and securely controlled opportunities to run. 5. Kombai The Kombai, or Combai, is another important native breed from Tamil Nadu. Historically associated with guarding and hunting, it has a stronger, more compact appearance than India’s lightly built sighthounds. In August 2026, ICAR-NBAGR registered the Kombai as an indigenous breed from Tamil Nadu, making it the sixth dog breed in the national registration system. Its traditional guarding background deserves attention. Confidence and territorial instincts can be valuable in a working dog, but those same characteristics require careful socialisation in a modern household. A prospective owner should therefore choose a Kombai because its temperament and needs suit their lifestyle, not simply because the breed is rare or historically important. 6. Gaddi Dog The Gaddi Dog comes from Himachal Pradesh and is closely associated with pastoral communities that move livestock through Himalayan terrain. Its traditional work was very different from that of a southern Indian sighthound. Rather than pursuing game, Gaddi dogs helped guard livestock in demanding mountainous environments. That required independence, confidence, endurance and the ability to respond to potential threats. These qualities can make livestock guardian breeds very capable working dogs but also more complicated urban pets. Climate is another serious consideration. A dog developed for Himalayan conditions cannot simply be grouped with every other “Indian breed” under the assumption that all native dogs are equally suited to India’s hottest cities. 7. Changkhi The Changkhi is associated with Ladakh and the Changthang region. Traditionally used by pastoral communities for livestock protection, the Changkhi developed in an environment dramatically different from India’s hot and humid plains. Its recognition in 2025 brought greater formal attention to one of India’s lesser-known native dog populations. For prospective owners, however, rarity should never be the main attraction. A high-altitude livestock guardian has specific climatic, behavioural and space requirements. The Changkhi is therefore better understood first as a specialised working breed rather than as an unusual pet for city life. 8. Kanni The Kanni is a sighthound associated with Tamil Nadu. Lean, agile and built for speed, it shares many functional characteristics with other southern Indian hunting hounds. Its traditional role means potential owners should expect an athletic dog rather than a passive house pet. Regular physical activity, secure exercise and early socialisation are important. Discussions around Kanni and Chippiparai classification can also become complicated, with breed names and coat varieties treated differently by different sources and communities. For prospective owners, understanding the dog’s actual lineage, temperament and working characteristics is more useful than arguing over labels alone. 9. Rampur Hound The Rampur Hound, often called the Rampur Greyhound, is associated with Rampur in Uttar Pradesh. It was historically developed as a hunting hound. Like other sighthounds, its body is built for efficient movement and speed. An adult Rampur may appear perfectly relaxed indoors and still require substantial opportunities for physical activity. Homes considering one should therefore have a realistic exercise plan and secure handling arrangements. 10. Bakharwal Dog The Bakharwal Dog is associated with pastoral communities in Jammu and Kashmir. It has traditionally been used for livestock guarding in Himalayan environments. Large livestock guardians tend to be independent, alert and protective because those characteristics were useful when working around animals and potential predators. That background is important for anyone considering such a dog purely as a family pet. Its heavier coat and regional adaptation also mean climate should be considered carefully. A dog’s country of origin does not tell you enough about the weather it is suited to. India contains everything from cold Himalayan environments to tropical coastal regions. 11. Jonangi The Jonangi is associated with southern India and is one of the country’s lesser-known native dog populations. It has traditionally been connected with working and guarding roles. Because breeds like the Jonangi are much less standardised and less commonly encountered than popular companion breeds, broad temperament claims should be treated cautiously. If you are considering one, learn as much as possible about the individual dog, its parents, its early socialisation and the environment in which it was raised. 12. Kaikadi The Kaikadi is associated particularly with Maharashtra and with communities that historically used dogs for hunting. It is generally described as a lean, active native dog. As with India’s other hunting types, its original purpose is more useful to prospective owners than a simple “loyal and intelligent” description. A dog bred to move, chase and work needs an owner prepared to provide exercise and structure. 13. Mahratta Greyhound The Mahratta Greyhound, or Mahratta Hound, represents another part of India’s regional sighthound tradition. Associated with Maharashtra, these dogs historically emphasised speed, agility and working ability rather than the highly uniform appearance expected in many modern show breeds. Exercise and prey drive are therefore more important ownership considerations than grooming. 14. Indian Spitz The Indian Spitz occupies a somewhat different position from ancient regional landraces and traditional working dogs. It became widely popular in India as a companion dog and is much more naturally associated with household life than breeds developed to hunt or protect livestock. Indian Spitz dogs tend to be alert and interactive and generally need regular walks, play, training and grooming. Their smaller size can make them easier to accommodate in an urban home than a large livestock guardian or highly athletic hound. However, small does not mean maintenance-free. Every dog still requires exercise, veterinary care, training, enrichment and attention. What About Other Indian Dog Breeds? India’s native dog heritage extends beyond the breeds above. Names such as Pashmi Hound, Banjara Hound, Pandikona, Bully Kutta, Himalayan Sheepdog or Bhutia, Haofa and Ramanathapuram Mandai appear in historical records, local traditions, dog-show circles and breed documentation. Some remain concentrated in particular regions. Others have small populations, inconsistent documentation or disagreements around classification. That is one reason a precise “total number of Indian dog breeds” is difficult to give. Instead of assuming that a breed not found on an official registry does not exist, it is better to distinguish between formal recognition and native population history. Why Isn’t the Indian Pariah Dog One of the Six ICAR-Registered Breeds? The Indian Pariah Dog is generally described as a landrace. A landrace develops over generations within a particular environment and population rather than through the tightly controlled breeding programme associated with many pedigree breeds. That helps explain why the Indian Pariah does not fit neatly into the same category as geographically defined and formally registered breeds such as the Rajapalayam or Mudhol Hound. Its lack of ICAR breed registration should not be mistaken for a lack of value. At Kannan Animal Welfare, many of the dogs we rescue and rehome are Indies or Indie mixes. Mansi arrived as a puppy, partially paralysed and barely responsive. After intensive care, she recovered and became a playful, curious dog who loves human company. Stories like hers matter because India’s native dogs should not only be discussed as genetic heritage. Many are living on streets or in shelters right now and need homes. If you cannot take one in, there are still simple ways to help street dogs in India. Are Indian Dog Breeds Better Suited to India’s Climate? You will often hear that Indian dogs are automatically better adapted to “Indian weather.” That statement needs context. India does not have one climate. A Chippiparai from Tamil Nadu, a Gaddi from Himachal Pradesh and a Changkhi from Ladakh developed under dramatically different environmental conditions. Short-coated dogs originating in warmer regions may cope differently with heat than heavily coated Himalayan breeds. Even dogs considered relatively heat-tolerant still need shade, drinking water, sensible exercise timing and protection during extreme temperatures. So the better question is not: “Is this an Indian dog?” It is: “What environment did this particular breed develop in, and does that match where I live?” Are Indian Dog Breeds Healthier Than Foreign Breeds? Another common claim is that Indian dogs have stronger immunity and rarely get sick. That is too simplistic. Some naturally developed populations may benefit from broad genetic diversity and the absence of extreme physical traits that cause problems in certain highly selected breeds. But nationality alone does not make a dog healthy. Genetics, breeding practices, nutrition, body condition, vaccination, parasite prevention, exercise, living conditions and access to veterinary care all matter. Native dogs can develop disease. Foreign breeds can live long, healthy lives when appropriately bred and cared for. A more responsible reason to consider an Indian breed is that its physical characteristics and historical working role may be better matched to your environment and lifestyle. Are Indian Dog Breeds Good Working Dogs? Yes. India’s native breeds have a long history of practical work. Different breeds were developed for hunting, guarding property, protecting livestock and accompanying pastoral communities. That working ability continues to attract institutional interest. Mudhol and Rampur Hounds, for example, have been used in Indian security-force dog programmes. This is useful evidence that native breeds can perform demanding roles. But working ability is also something prospective pet parents need to respect. A dog capable of intensive tracking, guarding or pursuit does not lose those needs simply because it now lives inside a house. Which Indian Dog Breed Is Right for Your Home? The best way to choose a dog is to start with your lifestyle rather than a photograph. Consider these factors before choosing any breed: Your home: A small flat can work for many individual dogs, but very large guardians and highly athletic hounds can be much harder to manage without adequate exercise and appropriate space. Your climate: Himalayan breeds and short-coated southern breeds have very different environmental histories. Your activity level: A Mudhol Hound or Chippiparai needs a very different routine from a less athletic companion dog. Your experience: Strong guarding instincts, prey drive and independence can be difficult for inexperienced handlers. Children and other pets: Individual temperament, socialisation and management matter. Breed alone cannot guarantee compatibility. If you already have animals at home, read our guide on how to introduce a rescued dog to your existing pets. Your time: Dogs need more than food and a morning toilet walk. Training, exercise and companionship are daily commitments. Why you want the dog: Rarity, appearance and social-media appeal are poor reasons to choose a breed. If your primary goal is simply a loving family companion, consider visiting a shelter before searching for a rare breed. You can see Kannan Animal Welfare’s dogs available for adoption and meet dogs whose personalities may already be known to their caregivers. Adopting an Indie vs Buying a Native Indian Breed There is nothing wrong with being interested in preserving a particular native breed. Responsible breeding can play an important role in protecting small regional populations. But preservation and commercial puppy production are not the same thing. If you specifically want a Rajapalayam, Mudhol, Kombai or another uncommon native breed, look carefully at how the dogs are bred and raised. Ask about the parents, health, temperament, living conditions and documentation. Be cautious of sellers whose main pitch is aggression, “purity,” rarity or exaggerated guarding ability. If what you really want is a companion, adoption may give you many more suitable choices. Our post on the nature and benefits of the Indie dog explains what to expect. Shelters frequently have adult Indies whose energy levels, size and personalities are already visible. That can make matching the dog to your household easier than choosing a young puppy based only on breed expectations. How to Care for Indian Dog Breeds Native dogs still require proper dog care. They need complete and balanced nutrition appropriate to their life stage, clean drinking water, vaccinations, parasite control, veterinary care, daily activity, training and social interaction. Our pet care guide for first-time pet owners in India covers these basics step by step. Exercise should be adapted to the dog. A young sighthound and an older rescued Indie should not be given identical routines simply because both are Indian dogs. Mental enrichment matters as well. Sniffing walks, training, interactive play, food enrichment and appropriate social experiences can be just as important as covering a fixed number of kilometres. You can read our detailed guide to feeding and caring for native Indian breeds for more practical advice. Why India’s Native Dog Breeds Matter Indian dog breeds represent much more than alternatives to Labradors, German Shepherds or Golden Retrievers. They are part of India’s living animal heritage. The Rajapalayam tells one story of Tamil Nadu. The Mudhol tells another from the Deccan. The Gaddi and Changkhi reflect pastoral life in Himalayan landscapes. The Indian Pariah represents something different again: generations of dogs living alongside human communities without being created by a modern pedigree system. Official recognition can help document and conserve rare populations. But conservation should not turn native breeds into fashion accessories. A rare working dog placed in an unsuitable urban household is not being preserved responsibly. Understanding what each dog was developed to do is just as important as celebrating where it came from. Frequently Asked Questions About Indian Dog Breeds How many Indian dog breeds are there? There is no universally agreed number because India has formally registered breeds, kennel-club breeds, regional populations and naturally developed landraces. More than 20 names appear across commonly cited lists and regional documentation. How many Indian dog breeds are registered with ICAR-NBAGR? As of August 2026, six indigenous dog breeds are registered through ICAR-NBAGR: Rajapalayam, Chippiparai, Mudhol Hound, Gaddi, Changkhi and Kombai. Which were the first Indian dog breeds registered by ICAR? Rajapalayam, Chippiparai and Mudhol Hound became the first three native dog breeds registered by ICAR-NBAGR in 2020. Which is the newest registered Indian dog breed? The Kombai of Tamil Nadu was registered in August 2026. Which Indian dog breed is suitable for an apartment? There is no breed that is automatically suitable for every apartment. Many Indies and Indian Spitz dogs can adapt successfully to urban homes when their individual energy levels and exercise needs are met. Highly athletic sighthounds and large livestock guardians are generally more demanding. Is an Indian Pariah Dog the same as a street dog? No. “Street dog” describes where a dog lives. Indian Pariah Dog refers to a native landrace or type. Street populations can contain Pariah-type dogs as well as dogs of mixed ancestry. Are Indian dogs healthier than foreign breeds? Not automatically. Genetics, responsible breeding, preventive veterinary care, nutrition and lifestyle all influence health. Some native populations may avoid certain problems associated with extreme breed traits, but Indian dogs can still develop illnesses. Are Indian dog breeds low-maintenance? Some short-coated native dogs have relatively simple grooming needs, but that does not make them low-responsibility pets. Exercise, training, healthcare, nutrition and companionship remain essential. Are Mudhol Hound and Caravan Hound the same? The names Mudhol Hound and Caravan Hound have historically been used for the same or closely identified Deccan sighthound population, although naming conventions can differ between sources and registries. ICAR-NBAGR uses the name Mudhol Hound for its registered breed. Which Indian dog breeds make good guard dogs? Several native breeds have histories connected with guarding, including Rajapalayam, Kombai, Gaddi and other livestock guardian populations. Strong guarding instincts also increase the importance of training, socialisation and responsible management. Should I adopt an Indie? If an Indie matches your household, lifestyle and experience, adoption can be an excellent option. Rather than choosing by breed label alone, meet the dog and discuss its temperament, energy level and history with the shelter or foster caregiver. The Indian Dog That Needs You May Already Be Waiting India’s native dogs deserve greater recognition. But recognising them should mean more than sharing photographs of rare breeds or celebrating an accession number. It should also mean making responsible choices about the dogs already around us. For someone with the right environment and experience, preserving a regional Indian breed can be meaningful. For many households looking for a companion, however, the right dog may already be waiting in a shelter. At Kannan Animal Welfare, rescued dogs arrive with very different histories. Some need medical rehabilitation. Others need time to learn that people can be trusted. Many simply need a home. You can see how donations help save these animals. If you are ready to bring a dog into your family, meet our dogs available for adoption. If adoption is not possible right now, you can still become a virtual parent and help support a sanctuary dog. These resilient, intelligent, and adaptable dogs have roamed the streets of India for centuries, thriving in diverse environments. Unlike purebred dogs, Indies are naturally evolved, making them hardy, low-maintenance, and well-suited to the Indian climate. Their sharp instincts, loyalty, and affectionate nature make them wonderful companions when given the right care and understanding. However, bringing home an Indie dog comes with unique considerations. These dogs, having lived a life on the streets tend to be amazingly clever. As a trainer, some of the smartest dogs I’ve ever worked with have been Indies – they learn quickly, are intelligent and great fun to train. But as with any smart dog, they need mental challenges to keep them happy. They don’t want to sit around all day. They want a job, a challenge, a reason to wake up every day. Even at that young age, I noticed that when I interacted with the stray dogs in my neighbourhood using simple routines, predictable gestures, and calm boundaries, the chaos of the street would dissolve into cooperation and understanding. Those early discoveries of mutual respect and structure became the foundation of what has now evolved into many years of work with dogs, humans, and communities. Decades later, I have worked with RWAs, pet parents, trainers, and caregivers across India—rehabilitating dogs from severe “red-zone” behaviour to stable, bite-free community members. Many of these dogs had histories as serious as mauling another animal or even injuring people, yet with structured systems they never repeated those behaviours. This guide is a distillation of those decades of fieldwork—written for community feeders, RWAs, and animal caregivers who want to prevent bite incidents, reduce conflict, and create true coexistence with our beloved Indie dogs. The starting point for any community is to take responsibility. Stray care is not only about dropping food; it is about accountability, structure, and compassion. A simple but effective first step is for each colony or block to conduct a census of its stray dogs. This census should not be a vague estimate but an organized record with photographs, age, sex, and temperament notes. A health ledger should be maintained—tracking sterilization, vaccinations, deworming, and tick control. RWAs should allocate a small annual budget for this purpose: covering sterilisation gaps, ensuring vaccinations, supporting medical treatment, and even basic training when needed. Partnerships with local vets or NGOs can further guarantee that help is available for sterilization drives and in emergencies. Feeding should be done with structure. Dedicated feeding sections/zones away from school gates, colony entrances, or traffic choke points. Fixed timings for feeding. Serve–supervise–sanitize. Dogs should eat calmly in as small groups as possible, bowls should be cleaned, and the space should remain hygienic. A more preferable method of feeding has been explained further in the article. The diet should be balanced—Rotating protein and carbohydrates or kibble, rather than feeding only leftovers. Teach Sit–Wait–Okay before meals. Reward calm behaviour away from gates. Desensitize to cycles, uniforms, delivery bags, etc. Manage in groups of 2–3. Read the training basics blog Medical kits in colonies Vet hotlines Transport plans Incident logs Indie or community dogs are often unfairly branded as aggressive or dangerous. These perceptions usually come from misunderstood behaviours. People complain of dog poop in public spaces, dogs chasing scooters, or barking at unfamiliar people. While these are real irritants, they are not insurmountable problems. Dog waste can be managed with proper clean-up systems, and chasing behaviour can be reduced with training and desensitisation. It is important to understand who Indies are. They are semi-wild, semi-urban dogs—descendants of India’s ancient Pariah dogs who have over the decades interbred with foreign breeds like Labradors, Retrievers, Pomeranians, and even Huskies. This has created a diverse genetic pool, with dogs retaining survival instincts that have not been shaped by selective breeding. They are naturally territorial and have a strong prey drive—meaning fast-moving objects like squirrels, cats, or scooters can trigger them to chase. This does not mean they are inherently dangerous; it means they are responding to instinct. The true danger, in my experience, lies in unchecked inbreeding. When sterilisation is ignored, siblings and relatives breed among themselves, producing unstable temperaments and highly reactive offspring. From my years of work, I can confidently say that most bite incidents involve inbred dogs rather than healthy Indies. This makes sterilisation not just an animal welfare necessity, but a public safety measure. While feeding is an act of kindness, overfeeding without structure often creates more problems than it solves. In nature, a dog’s ecology requires it to work daily for survival—scavenging, sniffing, and hunting. When a community feeder piles huge amounts of food in one place two or three times a day, dogs lose their natural outlet. They become jobless Indies—dogs with nothing left to do but sleep. This leads to resource guarding, territorial aggression, and even sleep aggression. A constantly well-fed dog spends more time resting around feeding points and reacts sharply when disturbed. Without the challenge of working for food, their energy turns inward, often expressed as reactivity. As the saying goes, an empty mind is a devil’s playground—and this holds true for dogs too. Feed strategically, not excessively. Feeding must also be coordinated among caregivers to avoid overlap. The focus should always be on maintaining a dog’s mental and physical balance, not creating entitlement. Conflict in colonies usually arises not because of the dogs themselves, but because of misunderstandings and lack of systems. Rule 20 of the Animal Birth Control Rules 2023, make it the responsibility of RWAs or local body representatives to ensure designation of adequate feeding zones/spots. Where a conflict arises between RWA/residents in this regard, the RWA must form an animal welfare committee to redress the situation. When RWAs and feeders work together, these conflicts can be diffused easily. Residents quickly notice when dogs are calmer, quieter, and less of a disruption, and that changes sentiment. The first step is a formal RWA–Feeder Pact: agreeing on Publish census with regular updates on sterilisation and vaccination progress. Designated feeding zones and times. Hygiene responsibility and poop-clean policies. Monthly training sessions with a canine behaviourist can teach residents how to respond to dogs calmly instead of with fear. Most friction points can be solved with simple systems. Dog attacks are rare, but they become headlines. To manage them, we must understand the triggers: territorial defense, resource guarding, maternal instinct, pain, fear, and above all inbreeding. Here are some tips: Stay calm. Don’t scream or run. Stand firm. Face them and hold your ground. Look bigger. Straighten up, widen posture. Use water. Splash if dogs come within 2–3 feet — this usually makes them back off and is most humane under the circumstances. Do not use sticks or stones. They don’t scare dogs and can cause the dog to react defensively, making the situation worse. Dogs signal their intent through body language: GROWLS or LUNGES means immediate space must be created. If there is a Bite Incident: Wash wound for 15 mins with soap and water. Apply antiseptic, seek rabies vaccine. Place dog under vet observation. Reset the zone where bite occurred: The site of the bite should also be reset—feeding paused, then resumed under supervision, with daily counter-conditioning to desensitize the dogs to whatever triggered the incident. With consistency, even red-zone spots can be stabilized. The key is not panic, but protocol. RWAs are the most critical pillar in community dog management. They set the tone for how citizens perceive dogs. Will ban feeding and spread anti-dog sentiment. Negative messaging snowballs: Adults panic at dogs, children are taught to scream or throw stones, and dogs respond with defensiveness. Fearful humans plus unmanaged dogs are the recipe for dog bites. Will conduct censuses, ensure sterilization, and hire trainers. The solution is structured space-sharing. One area can be dedicated for strays under the supervision of bonded feeders, others can be pet-friendly, and if the space allows it then there can be no-dog zones also. This balances everyone’s needs. RWAs should also invest in canine behaviourists—at just a fraction of the colony budget—to guide residents and prevent incidents. Every RWA and feeder group can commit to a simple but powerful framework. These steps cost little but create enormous change in how dogs and humans live together. When unmanaged, they can create friction. But with structured feeding, strict sterilization, training, and responsible RWAs, every colony can transform Indies into guardians instead of so-called ‘menaces.’ I have dedicated my life to proving this through seminars, workshops, rehabilitation projects, and direct community management. The system works. It is science, not sentiment. If adopted consistently, it will reduce bites & possibly eliminate them, change perceptions, and allow humans and dogs to coexist with respect and harmony. Instead of dumping food, I carried biscuits or pellets on long walks, feeding tidbits along a one- or two-kilometer route, or around the colony. This simple adjustment changed everything. Dogs no longer saw me as an ATM machine dispensing salary once or twice a day; they saw me as a leader, a guide who engaged with them. They followed me, listened to me, and responded when called—even if they had started chasing someone. This system created dogs that were not only protective of their colony but also controllable. They would ward off drunkards or petty criminals but would return to me when asked, preventing harm to innocent people. Such practices create trust not only between dogs and feeders, but also between feeders and the wider community, because residents see visible control and accountability. One of the few things that I like to train the dogs on, is responding to their names. All of us have names for our streeties, and teaching name response is a vital aspect of creating the bond. Additional tips: Use different tones of voice—happy, calm, loud, or whisper—to help the dog recognize their name in various contexts. Avoid repeating the name multiple times consecutively to prevent the dog from ignoring the call. Do not distract or punish the dog when they do not respond; instead, try training in a quieter place or repeat with patience. Whenever you have food in your hand, the simplest thing that a feeder can do is wait till the dog sits down. As soon as that happens, say ‘yes’ or ‘okay’, and that’s when you give the food. If followed consistently, with these basic changes, your community dogs would learn their name, they will come to you when called and they will sit during feeding time. And these are important aspects to coexist harmoniously in a community. In addition, I enjoy walking distances and feeding dogs. Instead of placing large piles of chicken and rice in one spot, I prefer to walk a few steps, feed the dogs, call them over, give them some tidbits, and then move further along. This approach creates a continuous, traveling bond between the strays and me, rather than making them overly protective of a single area. Dogs can sometimes become territorial about their feeding spots even when it’s not mealtime, and this method helps prevent that behavior. Most importantly, the same dog should not be fed by six, seven different people in an uncoordinated way. If a dog responds well to its name and has a reliable recall, it will come back when called — even if it’s chasing cars, bikes, or kids. If you’re nearby, whether standing on your balcony or just a little distance away, you can simply call out their name, and they’ll return to you. That is the primary advantage: coming back whenever they’re called. We should take responsibility and accountability for our stray dogs — ensuring their good behavior, good health, and sterilization. These three aspects should be part of our responsibility and accountability. We must aim to build a more active relationship with the dogs, fostering cooperation and obedience, instead of just dropping piles of food, taking a photo, and walking away. If you’re among the growing numbers opening their homes and hearts to Indie dogs – you have our full support! It’s heartening to see Indies finally receiving the love, care and pampering you will surely shower them with. However, if this is your first trip down the pet-parenthood lane, especially pet-parenthood, to an Indie, there are some things to keep in mind. Indies, while sturdy and resilient, come with a whole set of quirks of their own. With distinctive characters and unique personalities, it takes a loving, nurturing and patient environment for them to flourish and live their best life fully. But if you adopted an Indie under the assumption that they would be low-maintenance – you might have already realised that’s not necessarily the case! They’re adapted to local environments and less susceptible to breed-specific illnesses. However, they still have distinctive needs – although nothing a little love and patience can’t address. With decades of experience interacting with Indies, here’s what our team at Friendicoes believes every pet parent should know as they step into this journey. Getting to know your pup – temperament and behaviour Your recently adopted Indie pup may have some inherent behavioural tendencies due to their natural and survival instincts, and it’s best to understand and address these early on. How can you spot these behaviours? Spend quality time with your pup and observe them in various situations. Indies have an intense fight-or-flight response from surviving on the streets. Many of them can therefore be inherently nervous and skittish at first when introduced to home environments, new sounds and objects. Suppose you notice that this behaviour is not subsiding with time and find them to be continually anxious. In that case, it’s crucial to identify their triggers and help them overcome these fears with patience and training. Constant anxiety, as with any being, is detrimental to both their physical and mental health. Indies are pack animals that have also evolved to become considerably territorial. If you notice your pup growing overly protective of their home and family members and perhaps not allowing guests to come over – it’s important to help them understand that their space is not threatened. Left unchecked, this behaviour could lead to aggression in later years, as with any breed. Indies are among the most loyal dogs you will ever come across, and with the right help at the right time to adjust to home life, they make the most wonderful and loving companions. Indies are also known to be great with children, but it’s important to socialise them at an early age. Many Indies who are only exposed to family members tend to be far more wary and distrustful of other dogs and humans. Building a conducive environment and lifestyle To make sure you’re providing the most nurturing environment and lifestyle for raising your pup, here are a few tips to keep in mind: Give them a designated space to call their own. Indies, while being creatures of habit, are also territorial and tend to gravitate towards the same spots within each room. Initially, pick a quiet corner of the room and set it up for your pup with a bed. After a while, you might notice them choosing their own safe spaces, and you can reposition their beds to their liking. Regular vet trips are necessary for thorough health check-ups and annual vaccinations. If you have adopted an Indie pup from a shelter, don’t forget to carry any medical reports and records that have been shared with you about their history. Unpredictability can cause dogs some stress; therefore, it is important to establish and stick to a routine. They will take some time to get used to their new family, environment and lifestyle. It could take a few weeks or even a few months. Once they get the hang of the routine for feeding, walks/exercise, playtime and grooming, they’ll be prepared for what is to come as they go along their day. For Indies especially, exercise is super important. Indies, in general, are incredibly high on energy, so they need regular exercise daily to burn off the excess. They must also be frequently entertained with engaging and stimulating activities that occupy them for hours. So be prepared to get in your daily steps and have your creativity challenged as you take your pup for long walks, runs, games, activities and doggy dates. Start training them from Day 1. Indies are highly intelligent and easy to train. With just 10-15 minutes of daily training, they can pick up many tricks and commands. You can cover everything from basic commands like ‘sit’, ‘stay’, etc., to socialisation with humans and other dogs and behavioural training. For bonding purposes and to avoid confusion in their minds, it’s recommended that you take on this responsibility with your dog and, ideally, not pass on the training to a hired individual. With short coats that are mostly easy to maintain, you can stay on top of their basic grooming needs like bathing, brushing, and nail trimming at home without a hassle. However, if you’re hesitant to cut their nails by yourself, you can always treat them to a formal grooming session to avoid any mishaps. Be sure to indulge in positive reinforcement after grooming to ensure a pleasant experience and association for them. Home-cooked meals are the way to go. Indies are fuss-free regarding their nutrition, and you need to ensure that you’re feeding them healthy and balanced meals – easily achieved with Indian cooking. You can even experiment with the same after consulting your vet – but be careful about specific ingredients that are a no-no for dogs. While these tips will help you better understand your new baby and navigate the various responsibilities you hold, perhaps the most important thing to learn about Indies is this: given their inherently self-sufficient nature, their instincts with respect to their likes, dislikes, routine and lifestyle are unsurprisingly strong. They’re very in tune with their needs, and you must be perceptive, learn their communication cues and follow their lead. With time, you’ll find a routine that suits you both, and your trust in them will help build a bond like no other. Each dog’s temperament and needs will be unique, but we hope this gives you a better understanding of how to raise your Indie puppy. Caring for a dog is a big responsibility, and the puppy days, in particular, can seem chaotic and stressful at times. But we guarantee it’s always worth it in the end. The hectic days of the pup-parent life are to be enjoyed to the fullest and treasured, as you will dearly miss them as time passes. Patience, consistency, gentleness and a whole lot of love will guarantee you a happy and fulfilled pet parenting journey ahead!

Why Exercise is Non-Negotiable for Your Dog's Health Regular exercise is one of the most important things you can do for your dog's physical and mental health, and most Indian pet dogs are simply not getting enough of it. A dog that doesn't move enough doesn't just gain weight. They become bored, anxious, destructive, and sometimes aggressive. Think about it this way. Your dog has no phone, no TV, no way to entertain themselves beyond what their environment offers. Exercise is not just physical, it's their primary source of mental stimulation, social interaction, and emotional release. Whether you live in a small flat in Mumbai or a house with a garden in Bengaluru, there are ways to make sure your dog gets what they need. This guide covers exactly that. How Much Exercise Does a Dog Actually Need in India? Most adult dogs need between 30 minutes to 2 hours of exercise per day depending on their breed, age, and health status. There is no single number that works for every dog, but a good starting point is understanding where your dog falls on the energy spectrum.Here's a general guide by dog type: High energy breeds like Labrador Retrievers, Golden Retrievers, German Shepherds, Border Collies, and Huskies need 60 to 120 minutes of vigorous activity daily. A short walk around the block is not enough for these dogs. Medium energy breeds like Beagles, Cocker Spaniels, and Indie dogs of medium build do well with 45 to 60 minutes of moderate activity split across two sessions. Low energy breeds like Pugs, Shih Tzus, Bulldogs, and older dogs of any breed are happy with 20 to 30 minutes of gentle walking and some light play. Puppies need short, frequent bursts of play rather than long walks. A rough guide is 5 minutes of exercise per month of age, twice a day. So a 4-month-old puppy needs around 20 minutes per session. Senior dogs still need daily movement but at a gentler pace. Regular short walks help maintain joint mobility and mental sharpness. Age, health conditions, and the Indian climate all play a role too. On a 40 degree summer afternoon, even a high energy Labrador should not be out running. Timing and intensity matter as much as duration. Best Outdoor Exercises for Dogs in India The best outdoor exercises for dogs in India combine physical activity with mental stimulation, and work within the practical realities of Indian streets, parks, and weather. Daily WalksWalking is the foundation of every dog's exercise routine and it's more than just physical. A walk gives your dog the chance to sniff, explore, and mentally process their environment, which is genuinely tiring for them in the best way. Aim for at least two walks a day, morning and evening, when temperatures are cooler. In Indian cities, pavement quality, traffic, and stray dog encounters make walks more complex than in other countries. Keep your dog on a leash, carry water, and choose quieter routes where possible. Fetch and Retrieve GamesFetch is one of the most efficient ways to tire a dog out quickly. Ten minutes of fetch can equal 30 minutes of walking in terms of energy expenditure. Find an open area, a society compound, a park, or even a quiet road early in the morning, and let your dog sprint. Not all dogs fetch instinctively. If yours doesn't, start by rolling the ball along the ground and rewarding any interest in it. Most dogs pick it up with a little encouragement. SwimmingFor dogs that love water, swimming is one of the best full-body, low-impact exercises available. It's especially good for overweight dogs or dogs with joint issues because it builds muscle without stressing the joints. Labradors and Golden Retrievers in particular tend to love it. If you live near a beach, lake, or have access to a dog-friendly pool, this is worth exploring. Always supervise water sessions and rinse your dog thoroughly afterwards, especially after sea or pond water. Off-Leash Play With Other DogsSocialised dogs benefit enormously from free play with other dogs. The running, chasing, and wrestling they do together is far more vigorous than anything you can replicate on a leash. Dog parks and society play areas in Indian cities are becoming more common and are worth seeking out if your dog is well socialised and comfortable with other dogs. Indoor Exercise for Dogs in India: For Hot Days and Small Spaces Indoor exercise for dogs in India is essential, especially during peak summer months, monsoon season, and for pet parents living in apartments without easy outdoor access. The good news is that mental exercise can be just as tiring as physical exercise for dogs. A dog that has to think and problem-solve will be just as calm and content as one that has run for an hour.Try these at home: Staircase runs. If you live in a building, running up and down a few flights of stairs is a surprisingly effective workout for dogs. Start slow and keep sessions short. Hide and seek. Hide your dog's favourite toy or treats around the house and let them sniff it out. This engages their nose and brain simultaneously and most dogs absolutely love it. Tug of war. A good tug session with a rope toy gives your dog a physical workout and is great for bonding. Let them win sometimes. It builds confidence. Kong or puzzle feeders. Stuffing a Kong toy with food or using a snuffle mat at mealtimes turns eating into a mental workout. This is particularly helpful for anxious or bored dogs who tend to finish meals in seconds and then look for trouble. Training sessions. Teaching new commands or practising existing ones for 10 to 15 minutes is mentally exhausting for dogs in the best way. Sit, stay, roll over, find it, leave it. Even basic commands repeated in short sessions use a lot of brain energy. For more ideas on keeping your dog engaged and out of mischief, our blog on How to Handle a Hyperactive Dog: A Guide to Calming Your Furball has some useful tips that pair well with a solid exercise routine. Exercise for Overweight Dogs in India: Where to Start If your dog is overweight, exercise needs to be introduced gradually and gently to avoid putting stress on their joints and heart. Start with short, slow walks and build up duration and intensity over several weeks rather than jumping straight into vigorous activity. A few important things to keep in mind for overweight dogs: Walk in the coolest parts of the day, early morning or after sunset, to avoid overheating. Overweight dogs overheat much faster than lean dogs. Swimming is ideal if accessible, as it builds fitness without joint strain. Watch for signs of overexertion: heavy panting, lagging behind, lying down mid-walk, or excessive drooling. Stop and rest if you see any of these. Exercise alone won't fix obesity. Diet is equally, if not more, important. A calorie-appropriate, high-protein, low-filler diet combined with regular exercise is the most effective approach. Set small, consistent goals. An extra 5 minutes of walking per week adds up quickly over a month. Lickicious is made with real chicken and fish as primary ingredients, without unnecessary fillers, supporting a lean, healthy body condition alongside regular exercise. Explore our adult dog food range to find the right fit for your dog. Exercising Your Dog in Indian Weather: Practical Tips India's extreme heat, humidity, and monsoon season make year-round outdoor exercise challenging, and adjusting your routine to the weather is just as important as the exercise itself. Summer (April to June). Walk only in the early morning before 8am or after 7pm when the sun is down. Pavement heat is a serious concern, test the ground with your hand. If it's too hot for your palm for 5 seconds, it's too hot for your dog's paws. Monsoon (July to September). Watch for waterlogged streets and leptospirosis risk from contaminated puddles, a bacterial infection dogs can pick up through contact with infected water. Dry your dog's paws thoroughly after every walk. Winter (November to February). This is the best time for longer, more vigorous outdoor exercise in most Indian cities. Early morning walks in cool, crisp air are genuinely enjoyable for most dogs and their pet parents. For more on keeping your pet safe through seasonal changes, read our blog on Weathering the Storm Together: A Guide to Monsoon Pet Care. Fun Activities for Dogs in India Beyond the Usual Walk Beyond daily walks and fetch, there are several engaging activities for dogs in India that provide richer physical and mental stimulation and strengthen the bond between you and your pet. Agility training at home. Set up a simple obstacle course using cushions, chairs, and cardboard boxes. Guide your dog through with treats. It's surprisingly effective and very entertaining for both of you. Nose work. Hide treats or a scented item in different rooms and let your dog sniff them out. Dogs have an extraordinary sense of smell and using it is deeply satisfying for them. Pet-friendly travel and trails. India's growing pet travel scene means more dog-friendly cafes, beaches, and hill stations than ever before. A weekend trip with your dog is one of the richest experiences you can give them. Our blog on The Best Destinations for Dogs in India: Exploring Pet-Friendly Places] has some great options to explore. Doggy playdates. Arranging regular playdates with a friend's or neighbour's dog gives your pet social exercise and mental stimulation that solo walks simply can't match. FAQs How much exercise does a dog need in India every day?Most adult dogs need between 30 minutes to 2 hours of exercise daily depending on breed and age. The Basics Pet owners should: read a label correctly select a food labeled for the pet’s species, life stage and condition follow feeding directions on the label The nutritional adequacy statement—usually found in small print on the back or side of pet food packaging—is the key to meeting a pet’s nutritional needs. For more about the nutritional adequacy statement, click here. A variety of retailers—from grocery stores to specialty shops to websites—sell an abundance of pet food products. All options that are compliant with the regulatory requirements should be safe and nutritious. Species Pet food should provide a dog or cat proper nutrition. Because dogs and cats have different nutrient requirements, pet food must be formulated for the intended species. For example, cats require nutrients, such as taurine and ‘pre-formed’ Vitamin A, that dogs do not. Life Stage and Condition Pet food should also supply a pet with a complete and balanced diet for its life stage and condition. “Complete” means the product contains all the nutrients required. “Balanced” means the nutrients are present in the correct ratios. The recognized life stages for both dogs and cats are: gestation/lactation (pregnancy and nursing) growth (includes kittens and puppies) maintenance all life stages Different quantities and ratios of nutrients as well as different feeding rates are ideal for different life stages. An active, growing puppy or kitten needs nutrients in different quantities and ratios than a mature pet. Calorie-rich foods designed for young animals may make a less active adult animal obese. On the other hand, a service, hunting or working dog or a pregnant or nursing pet may not receive enough nutrition from a food designed for a sedentary adult house pet. Feeding Directions Even once a pet owner has selected the right pet food, if the pet eats too much or too little it isn’t receiving a complete and balanced diet. Some products provide feeding tables; others provide basic text instructions. Products labeled for ‘all life stages’ should have different feeding directions for gestation/lactation, growth and maintenance. Feeding directions for a complete and balanced food must specify, for the animal’s life stage, at least the amount of the food (usually in cups or cans) to give per weight of the animal per unit of time. For example, a product’s label may suggest that a 10- to 15-pound adult dog eat ½ cup twice a day to maintain its condition or body weight. Pet owners should remember that feeding directions are guidelines that may need revising based on a particular animal’s activities and condition. If an animal is gaining or losing weight, it is either getting too much or too little food and its intake should be adjusted accordingly. Treats and Supplements: Not Complete Foods Products not intended to be complete feeds are considered treats or supplements. These products are generally intended to be fed in addition to a complete diet (though exceptions exist). These products may be labeled as treats, supplements, with words of similar designation, or with the direction “for intermittent or supplemental feeding only.” In general, treats and supplements will be labeled with some basic nutritional information, but won’t contain a nutritional adequacy statement.
